catalog_quote: [p. 82, §4.3.2.1] Impressionistically, stress seems to fall on the penultimate syllable, generally being the final prefix before the stem. However, some differences in stress realization were found among different vowels, and it also seemed to depend on the number of syllables in the given word, in some cases. [p. 89, §4.4.1] This data shows that the vowels in Hän can receive either syllable or stem stress, but probably not both. Syllable stress tends to occur on the penultimate syllable, or the final prefix before the stem, which causes vowel lengthening. This syllable stress tends to lengthen full vowels to almost the length of stressed stem vowels, and as a result, two syllable words almost seem to display equal stress on both syllables. More relevant to this study, however (considering the details of the Hän stress system have not yet been described) is the relationship between stem vowels and unstressed prefix vowels, where we can clearly see the effect of stem stress. [p. 1, abstract] Observations in many studies of Athabascan languages (Kari 1990, Tuttle 2005, Rice 2005, Leer 2005) have indicated that the stem syllable receives stress ... The results show that the most regular and predictable of these stress-induced effects is the increase in duration of segments in stem onsets (consonants) and nuclei (vowels). [p. 77, §4.3.1.1.1] This would indicate that stems cannot receive additional word-level, rhythmic stress, so the original measurements hold

new_statements.rule_in_words: Two layers: (i) morphological 'stem stress/prominence' — the stem syllable (word-final in this prefixing language; suffixes only vestigial) is reliably prominent, realised chiefly as longer stem-onset consonants and stem vowels; (ii) an impressionistic word-level 'rhythmic/syllable stress' on the penultimate syllable (the last prefix before the stem), which lengthens full prefix vowels to near stem-vowel length; reduced prefix /ə/ normally does not take it (CəCV words stressed on the final/stem syllable) except when the stem bears low tone, in which case the penult /ə/ is stressed. Hän is also tonal (unmarked/high vs. marked low). The author states the Hän word-stress system has not yet been fully described.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit secondary-stress rule; p. 101 says it is 'sometimes unclear which syllables are expected to receive primary and secondary stress'. Effect of penult rhythmic stress on full vowels may be reduced when the antepenult also has a full vowel (p. 85).
new_statements.exceptions: Reduced vowel /ə/ in prefixes avoids rhythmic stress (CəCV → stress on 2nd syllable) unless the following stem syllable has low tone, e.g. /əʔàw/ 's/he is eating', /načʼəʔàw/ with penult stress vs. /əjį/ 's/he has', /jəna/ 's/he is drinking' without (p. 79). Disyllabic monomorphemic stems (/jəje/ 'man', /t'əga/ 'girl') do not show stem-onset lengthening on their second syllable (pp. 98-99).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; tokens were words elicited inside carrier sentences from 3 Eagle-dialect speakers and 1 Dawson (Klondike-Moosehide) speaker. 'Stem stress' is morphological prominence measured acoustically (duration); 'syllable/rhythmic stress' is the author's perception plus vowel-duration measurements. The document read is the annotated ANLA draft; the deposited final thesis (ScholarWorks@UA uaf_grad_linguistics/19) could not be downloaded, so pagination refers to the draft.
new_statements.identity_note: Manker's data come from three Eagle, Alaska (Eagle dialect) speakers and one Dawson/Klondike-Moosehide (Yukon) speaker; both are dialects of Hän (hann1241), no separate glottocodes. The document quoted is the annotated ANLA draft (titled 'An Acoustic Study of Morphological Stress in Hän Athabascan') of the 2012 UAF M.A. thesis 'An acoustic study of stem prominence in Hän Athabascan'.

new_statements.quote: This acoustic study of the Hän language investigates the synchronic realization of this morphological conditioning in fricatives, stops, and vowels, and attempts to unify several different phonological effects into a single theory of stem prominence. The results show that the most regular and predictable of these correlates of stem prominence is the increase in duration of segments in stem onsets (consonants) and nuclei (vowels).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Abstract only: the stem syllable carries phonetic prominence, most reliably as increased duration of stem onset consonants and stem vowels; the abstract does not use the word 'stress' and gives no rule for word-level (syllable) stress placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the abstract. (The annotated draft of the same thesis, HN012M2012, already held by the project, describes a second, 'rhythmic' or 'syllable' stress on the penultimate syllable = final prefix before the stem, p.82 and p.89, and treats stem stress and syllable stress as normally not co-occurring.)
new_statements.exceptions: None in the abstract. (Draft, p.82: realization of penultimate stress varies by vowel quality and by number of syllables in the word; /a/ prefixes rarely receive stress, full vowels do.)
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis data are from Hän as spoken in Eagle, Alaska / Dawson area speakers per the draft; the abstract names no dialect.

new_statements.quote: [p. 97-98, sec. 4.4.1 'Duration'] The inconsistency of this data may suggest there is another uncontrolled variable affecting vowel duration. My own impressions corroborate this theory, as some prefixes seem longer in duration than others. This variable is most likely stress. As there has been no thorough description of stress in Han, it was impossible to remove this variable from the data without first conducting a separate study to fully understand this phenomenon. [p. 98] ... neither the preceding vowel (whether stressed, unstressed, full or reduced), nor the vowel or syllable weight of the stem seems to have any effect on stem prominence, which is entirely morphologically conditioned.

new_statements.relation_note: Same morphological (stem-prominence) type as the catalog record (classification morphological, rule empty) and as both existing statements; confirms duration as the main correlate and adds that stem prominence is exceptionless and independent of syllable weight and of the preceding vowel. Difference to note: the catalog's quote ('Impressionistically, stress seems to fall on the penultimate syllable..'; 'Syllable stress tends to occur on the penultimate syllable') comes from the annotated DRAFT (ANLA HN012M2012); the final deposited thesis does not contain that passage and instead states that stress in Hän has not been described and must be studied separately, keeping only example (4.1) wher…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence in Hän is stem (morphological) prominence: stem-onset consonants and stem-nucleus vowels are regularly and significantly longer than prefix segments, in every environment, regardless of the preceding vowel or the stem's syllable weight; duration is the most regular correlate (sec. 5.1). Word-level stress is explicitly treated as a separate, not-yet-described system: the author says there is no thorough description of stress in Hän, that some prefix full vowels impressionistically carry stress (lengthening them), and defers the stress system to future research (sec. 4.5, 5.3.1). Example (4.1), p. 99, marks impressionistic primary stress on the pre-stem (penultimate) syllable in /le.jih.ja.'ni.shat/ 'they fell in love with each other' and /wa.'ne.shaw/ 'it was hot', with the stem also prominent ('almost like a spondee in the last two syllables').
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 99: in (4.1a) 'there seems to be some, possibly secondary, stress on the syllable /jih/ and a little more, perhaps primary stress, on the syllable /ni/, despite the lower tone' -- an impression on one example, not a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is said to fall on full vowels and rarely on reduced vowels (p. 98, citing Kari 1990, Tuttle 1998, 2003, Hargus 2007 for Athabascan generally); stem prominence has no exceptions ('does not fail to occur in any sort of environment', p. 98). Disyllabic stems (sec. 5.3.2, p. 109) are flagged as an open question.
new_statements.identity_note: Hän (Han Athabascan), primarily the Eagle, Alaska dialect (speakers recorded for the thesis; Dawson dialect differences noted in sec. 1.5 and 4.1.1.1).
